title: CDN and edge caching
tagline: Serve bytes from a server a few milliseconds from the user, and let the origin see only the misses.
why:
Light is slow at planet scale. A round trip from Singapore to a server in the US east coast is about 220 ms, and a new HTTPS connection needs two or three of those before the first byte: TCP, TLS, then the request itself. A CDN puts caching servers (points of presence, PoPs) in hundreds of cities, so a user in Singapore talks to a PoP in Singapore, a few milliseconds away.

The second win is load. Static files (JS, CSS, images, video segments, a public page) are identical for every user. If the edge answers 95% of those requests, the origin serves one request in twenty and its outbound bandwidth drops by the same factor. A national SMS blast with a link in it becomes a CDN problem, not an origin outage.

The interview questions are about the cache rules: what is cacheable, what the cache key is, how long entries live, and how you get a bad file out of 300 PoPs quickly.
how:
Routing. The CDN hostname resolves, through GeoDNS or anycast, to a nearby PoP. TLS ends there, so the expensive handshake happens over a 5 ms hop, not a 220 ms one.

Pull-through cache. The PoP looks up the cache key (by default host + path + query, plus any headers named in Vary). On a hit it answers from memory or SSD. On a miss it fetches from the origin, stores the response if the headers allow it, and returns it. The sim above is the same mechanism: read "database" as "origin". Skewed traffic means a small cache still gets a high hit rate.

Origin shield. A regional mid-tier cache between the PoPs and the origin. Without it, a new file misses in every PoP and the origin gets hundreds of identical requests. With it, they collapse into one.

Freshness is set by the origin's headers.

  • Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable for fingerprinted files like app.3f9a.js. The name changes when the content changes, so they never need purging.
  • s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=30 for HTML and public API responses: the edge keeps them a minute and refreshes in the background.
  • private or no-store for anything per user. Never let a response with Set-Cookie or account data into a shared cache.

Invalidation. Prefer versioned file names and short TTLs on the few files that point to them (the HTML). Use the CDN's purge API (by path, or by tag on CDNs that support surrogate keys) for mistakes and urgent takedowns.

Private content. Signed URLs or signed cookies with a short expiry let the edge serve a file only to the user who was given the link.

flows.name: Edge hit
flows.desc: The common case for static files.

steps.note: The CDN hostname resolves to a PoP near the user. DNS answers are cached, so this costs nothing on most requests.
The browser opens TLS to the Singapore PoP: a ~5 ms round trip instead of ~220 ms to a US origin.
The cache key /app.3f9a.js is in the PoP: a hit. Fingerprinted files can be cached for a year because a new build gets a new name.
Bytes come back from the edge. The origin never sees this request.

flows.name: Miss to origin
flows.desc: First request for a new file.

steps.note: A request for a file this PoP has not seen, or whose TTL ran out.
Miss at the edge. Ask the regional shield, not the origin, so 300 PoPs missing at once become one request.
Miss at the shield too. One request goes to the origin. CDNs also collapse concurrent misses for the same key into a single fetch.
The origin answers with Cache-Control. That header, not the CDN, decides whether and for how long the response is cached.
The shield stores it and passes it down; the PoP stores it too.
This user paid for the full trip. Every later user near this PoP gets a hit.

flows.name: Deploy and invalidate
flows.desc: Getting new content out to every PoP.

steps.note: Upload the new build first. New JS and CSS get new fingerprinted names, so nothing cached is wrong yet.
Only /index.html, which points at the new names, needs purging. Purge a few paths or a tag, not /*.
The CDN fans the purge out to every PoP. Depending on the provider this takes from under a second to a few minutes, so do not rely on it being instant.
The next request for /index.html misses and fetches the new version. Old JS files stay cached, which keeps users with the old page working.

tradeoffs.pro: Near 100% hit rate and no purges needed for static assets.
tradeoffs.con: Needs a build step that fingerprints files, and the HTML that references them must stay short-lived.

tradeoffs.pro: Staleness is bounded without any purge logic; good for public HTML and API responses.
tradeoffs.con: More misses and more origin load; a cold PoP refetches often.

tradeoffs.pro: Long TTLs on content that changes rarely, fresh within seconds when it does.
tradeoffs.con: Purges are eventually consistent across PoPs, may be rate limited or billed per path, and are easy to forget in a new code path.

tradeoffs.option: Cache dynamic or per-user responses at the edge
tradeoffs.pro: Large latency and load win for read-heavy APIs.
tradeoffs.con: One mistake in the cache key serves one user's data to another. Only with a key that includes the identity, or not at all.

numbers: Round trip Singapore to US east: about 220 ms; Singapore to a local PoP: 1 to 5 ms. On top of the TCP handshake, TLS 1.3 adds 1 round trip and TLS 1.2 adds 2.
Typical cache hit ratio for fingerprinted static assets: 95 to 99%. At 95%, the origin serves 1 request in 20.
Bandwidth: a 1 MB page weight × 1M visits = 1 TB. At a 95% byte hit ratio the origin sends 50 GB of it.
Origin shield: 300 PoPs missing on a new file become about 1 origin request per shield instead of 300.
Common TTLs: 1 year for fingerprinted files, 60 s plus stale-while-revalidate for public HTML, 0 (private) for anything per user.
say: Static assets go through a CDN with fingerprinted file names and a one-year TTL, so a deploy never needs a purge; only the HTML is short-lived.
I'll put an origin shield in front of the origin so a new file that misses in every PoP turns into one origin request, not hundreds.
Anything per user is marked private and bypasses the shared cache. Private files are served with short-lived signed URLs.
pitfalls: Caching a response that carries Set-Cookie or account details at a shared key. The next user gets someone else's session or data.
Purging /* on every deploy. Every PoP goes cold at once and the origin takes the full load, which is the outage the CDN was meant to prevent.
A cache key that includes junk query parameters (utm_source, timestamps). Each variant is a separate miss and the hit rate collapses. Normalise or strip them.
Forgetting the origin still needs capacity for a cold cache or a CDN outage. Size it for the miss rate you would see after a purge, not the steady state.
Assuming purges are instant and global. They take time to reach every PoP; design so stale content for a minute is harmless.

quiz.q: You ship a new app.js and some users still get the old one for an hour. What is the cleanest fix for the next deploy?
options: Set a 0 s TTL on all JS
Fingerprint file names (app.3f9a.js) and keep the HTML short-lived
Turn off the CDN for JS
quiz.why: A new build gets a new file name, so nothing cached is ever wrong. Only the HTML that points at it needs a short TTL. Purging everything or a 0 s TTL throws away the CDN's benefit.

quiz.q: A new file goes viral and the origin sees hundreds of identical requests within a second, one from each PoP. What prevents this?
options: An origin shield (mid-tier cache) with request collapsing
quiz.why: All PoPs miss on a new file. A shield gives them one shared parent, so the origin sees one fetch; collapsing merges concurrent misses for the same key.

quiz.q: Which response is most dangerous to cache at the CDN?
options: GET /account that returns the logged-in user's profile
quiz.why: A per-user response at a shared cache key leaks one user's data to the next. Mark it private or no-store.

quiz.q: Your CDN hit ratio is 40% on product images. The logs show URLs like /img/7.jpg?utm_source=sms&t=1731999. What is the likely cause?
options: TLS is ending at the origin
Query parameters make every request a different cache key
quiz.why: The default cache key includes the query string. Tracking parameters and timestamps make each request unique. Strip or ignore them in the cache key.
